steps.say: You just found two numbers from a target product (15) and a target sum (8). That hunt is the whole engine of factorising \(ax^2+bx+c\): the product you aim for is \(a \times c\), and the sum you aim for is the middle number \(b\). The rest is splitting and bracketing.

method_card.title: Factorising quadratics (a ≠ 1)
method_card.content:
When \(a \neq 1\) you cannot just find two numbers that multiply to \(c\); you must aim for the product \(ac\). This is the ac method, or splitting the middle term.

Find two numbers that multiply to \(ac\) and add to \(b\), rewrite the middle term as those two terms, then factorise in pairs and pull out the shared bracket. Always expand your answer to check it gives the original quadratic.
method_card.example:
Factorise \(3x^2 + 10x + 3\)

\(ac = 9\); two numbers multiply to 9 and add to 10: 1 and 9. Split: \(3x^2 + x + 9x + 3 = x(3x+1) + 3(3x+1)\). Answer: \((x+3)(3x+1)\).

steps: Multiply a by c. With larger leading numbers the product can be big, so list the factor pairs carefully.
Pick the pair that multiplies to \(ac\) and adds to b, choosing signs so the product and the sum both come out right.
Split, group in pairs, pull out the common bracket, then expand to check.
gold.title: Gold: large products and mixed signs

steps: Multiply a by c (the number in front of \(x^2\) times the constant). This is your target product.
Find two numbers that multiply to that product and add to the middle number b. With all-positive terms both numbers are positive.
Split the middle term into those two pieces, then factorise in pairs to reveal the shared bracket.

steps.content: Two numbers multiply to 6 and add to 7: \(6\) and \(1\).

steps: Multiply a by c as before, but watch the sign: a negative constant makes the product negative.
Find two numbers that multiply to that product and add to b. A negative product means one number is positive and one is negative.
Split the middle term and factorise in pairs, keeping every sign as you go.
